newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay shares end up despite rail freight hike.
newsitem.headline: Bombay shares end up despite rail freight hike.

text.p: Stocks drifted in lacklustre trade at Bombay bourses on Wednesday, with the announcment of India's railway budget having little impact on the market, dealers said.

The Indian government plans to raise freight rates by 12 percent for all commodities, barring essentials, for all distances, the Press Trust of India quoted Railway Minister Ram Vilas Paswan as saying while presenting his 1997/98 budget.
"The market was expecting a hike of 12-15 percent," said chief dealer Ketan Jhaveri at local brokerage Kotak Securities.
The Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) top 30-share index ended 9.67 points higher to 3,366.50 in a day of rangebound trade.

The increased freight rates which exclude 15 essential items such as foodgrains and pulses, edible oils, kerosene, sugar liquefied petroeum gas, fruits and jaggery will come into force from April 1, 1996, railway minister Paswan said. Producers said the hike would hurt manufacturers of commodity products such as steel, cement and plastics most.

"It would push up prices of most goods," said Anil Singhvi, treasurer at Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd, a leading cement maker. He said most industry officials had been expecting an 8.0-10.0 percent freight hike.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram will present the centre-left coalition government's 1997/98 (April-March) budget on Friday.

Minimal market expectations from the budget include scrapping a double taxation on company dividends, allowing firms to buy back their shares. They also hope for a reduction of a 7.5 percent corporate surcharge and reconfiguring a new minimum alternate tax, both of which were included in the last budget.
Among pivotals, Reliance rose 2.25 rupees to 264.0, SBI 0.75 to 274.75 and Tata Power 4.75 to 131.0 rupees.
